title: Sanitising equipment and parts: immersion, spray, air-drying and handling
audience: Cleaners and kitchen or processing staff who sanitise utensils, parts and equipment after washing.
learningOutcomes: Choose immersion, spray or wipe sanitising to suit the size and fixed or loose nature of the item.
Explain why sanitised items are air-dried rather than towel-dried.
Verify hot-water sanitising with a thermometer and a timer.
Store sanitised items so they cannot be contaminated again before use.

instruction.heading: Choose the sanitising method for the item
instruction.body: Loose utensils and small parts are dipped into a sanitising solution or hot water for the period the procedure sets. Fixed plant, including belts, saws and tables, is sprayed with a hand-pumped unit in a small operation, or with a pressurised unit in a large facility. A hand-held spray bottle does table sanitising in a restaurant. For hot-water sanitising, Queensland Health's cleaning and sanitising guidance gives a hot-water temperature of 77 degrees Celsius held for a minimum of 30 seconds.

instruction.heading: Let the surface air-dry
instruction.body: After the sanitising contact time, the surface is left to air-dry. Drying with a towel can carry microorganisms from the cloth or from the hands onto a surface that was just sanitised. Parts that cannot be immersed must be sprayed to cover the full surface, and enough solution must be applied to stay wet for the contact time. A surface that dries too fast before the contact time has ended has not been sanitised.

instruction.heading: Handle and store sanitised items
instruction.body: Sanitised items are stored on a clean rack or shelf, not on a bench that has not been sanitised. Keep sanitised parts apart from raw materials, and keep tools colour-coded by zone so that a tool used in one area is not carried into another. The colour-coding principle is covered in “Colour-coded cloths: a business-set system that keeps areas apart”. The person handling sanitised items should wash their hands before touching them, as the site procedure requires.

procedure: Confirm the item has been washed and rinsed, and that no soil is visible.
Choose immersion, spray or wipe according to the item and the site procedure.
For hot-water sanitising, check the water temperature with a thermometer and start the timer when the target is reached.
Immerse or spray the item for the full contact time, covering all surfaces.
Allow the item to air-dry on a clean rack.
Store the item in a clean location, separate from raw materials and unclean surfaces.
Record the method, the temperature or concentration, the contact time and the zone.

workedExamples.situation: A commercial kitchen works with a sink of four bays. After the wash and rinse compartments, a cook moves a stack of boards to the sanitising compartment, then takes them out and dries them with a clean towel.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is wrong with the drying step, and what should happen?
workedExamples.reasoning: Towel-drying can re-contaminate the boards. The boards should be air-dried on a clean rack after the full contact time, and the water temperature should have been checked with a thermometer.

equipmentAndPpe: Pump sprayer or high-pressure sprayer, as the site provides
Heat-resistant gloves, apron and eye protection

commonErrors.error: Sanitising a surface that still has visible soil.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean and rinse first, confirm no soil is visible, then sanitise.

commonErrors.error: Drying with a towel after sanitising.
Immersing only part of an item, or spraying only one face.
commonErrors.prevention: Cover all surfaces for the full contact time, turning the item where needed.
Check it with a thermometer and time the step from the point the target is reached.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hot water can cause scalds, so treat every hot tank, rinse and sanitising bath as a scald hazard. Use heat-resistant gloves and do not reach over steaming tanks.
Chemical sanitiser sprays and mists can irritate the eyes and airways. Wear eye protection and avoid breathing the mist.
Use the site's food-safety plan and confirm before relying on any figure.

qualityStandard: The item is clean and rinsed before sanitising starts.
The temperature or concentration and the full contact time are verified and recorded.
The item is air-dried, not towel-dried.
The sanitised item is stored apart from raw materials and unclean surfaces.
documentationEvidence: Method, temperature or concentration, and contact time for each batch.
Any item rejected for soil or incomplete sanitising, and the action taken.
summary: Sanitise only clean items, and cover every surface for the full contact time.
Use a thermometer and a timer; do not estimate.
Air-dry; never towel-dry a sanitised item.
Store sanitised items away from raw materials and unclean surfaces.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the preferred way to dry sanitised utensils?
options: Wipe them with a clean towel
Rinse in tap water, dry with a cloth
Let them air-dry on a clean rack
Blow them dry with the air hose

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a thermometer used for hot-water sanitising?
options: To make the water taste better and to keep the sinks looking clean
To cool the water before the rinse and to keep the sinks cool
To meet a rule about water colour and to note the colour in the log
To confirm the water reaches the required temperature for the set time

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the risk if sanitised parts are placed on an unclean bench?
options: They can be re-contaminated before use
Nothing, because sanitised items are sealed
